extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in history, media ethics, and the journalism/academic community (historians, journalists, general public)
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological news account tracking the development, reactions, and institutional consequences of a historian's plagiarism allegations; useful for understanding how media, universities, publishers, and peers evaluate alleged scholarly misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing appropriate credit to the source
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard to be met in every instance is providing appropriate credit to the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page quotes Goodwin saying this is the most important standard; surrounding discussion addresses whether footnotes, end-note anchors, or textual attribution satisfy this standard and notes that credit must be clear even when narrative flow is a concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper marking of quotations in notes and drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations must be properly marked in notes and working materials to avoid accidental appropriation when drafting the final manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin explained her mistake as 'not properly marking quotations in her 900 pages of hand-written notes.' The implication/guidance is that disciplined note-taking and clear demarcation of source verbatim text is required to prevent later misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between paraphrase and quotation (and when paraphrase requires credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrasing still requires attribution and must be sufficiently original; common expressions or necessary chronology may resemble sources, but appropriation of distinctive phrasing is problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin's defense cites 'common expression' and structural/chronological limits as possible reasons for resemblance; critics argue that close paraphrase or near-identical phrasing even with footnotes is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of appropriation as evidentiary factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer volume of verbatim or nearly verbatim words taken from another work supports claims of infringement or serious appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lynne McTaggert's op-ed: 'the sheer volume of the appropriation — thousands of my exact or nearly exact words — that supported my copyright infringement claim.' The page emphasizes quantity (number of pages/phrases) as strengthening allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes alone do not excuse verbatim or close textual copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding footnotes after the fact does not eliminate the problem when large passages remain presented as the author's own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics (Timothy Noah) argue that 'the addition of a few footnotes did not change the fact that numerous passages ... remained in Goodwin's text as if they were Goodwin's own.' Use of footnotes must be accompanied by correct quotation/clear attribution for verbatim/close wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harvard disciplinary policy for suspected misuse of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors must report suspected cases to the Dean; most cases are adjudicated by the Administrative Board and can result in required withdrawal for at least two semesters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted Harvard policy and commentator comparisons indicate formal institutional procedures and potentially severe penalties even for students; used as a standard of expected consequences in academic settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and culpability under academic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some academic standards (as represented by Harvard) do not make intent dispositive; unintentional misuse may be punished less harshly but intent is not always a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate cited on whether Goodwin's lack of intent (faulty note-taking) should excuse her; Noah notes Harvard punishes regardless of intent though penalties may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party source verification and independent review
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent checking of footnotes and source material (e.g., by outside readers or law firms) is a recognized method to assess the integrity of scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: LA Times contracted an outside reader to compare passages; Ropes & Gray reviewed footnotes and sources and issued a 'clean bill of health' for No Ordinary Time. Such reviews can either vindicate or further implicate an author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and disclosure of evidence by journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and publications have an obligation (per some critics) to disclose the underlying parallels/evidence so readers can judge the degree of copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philip Nobile criticized the LA Times for not publishing the 30-odd parallels its researcher found; debate about what newspapers should reveal about evidence in such disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty to label satire/humor clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must explicitly label satire to prevent readers from mistaking humorous pieces for factual reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NYT correction after a satirical Week in Review piece led readers to take allegations as factual; the correction noted the author was identified as a humor writer and the placement was in a position usually reserved for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/civic responses as measures of reputational consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawal of speaking invitations, stepping down from boards, or canceling keynote appearances are standard institutional reactions to serious allegations and serve as measures of reputational impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PBS leave of absence, universities (Delaware, James Madison University, University of Kansas, Wisconsin-Whitewater, NCUR) withdrawing invitations, and Goodwin's resignation from the Pulitzer Board cited as institutional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remediation by publishers (recall/pulping and corrected editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may respond by withdrawing/recalling tainted copies and issuing corrected editions; failure to follow through can be criticized as insufficient remediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin announced Simon & Schuster would destroy copies and publish a corrected edition; later reporting found uncorrected paperbacks still for sale, prompting criticism that the promised remediation was not fully carried out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-by-side textual comparison as indicator of copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct side-by-side comparisons showing near-identical phrasing or sentences are strong indicators of copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LA Times and Weekly Standard provided examples of parallel passages (e.g., photographer anecdote) that critics used to argue copying; the practice of juxtaposing passages is a common evidentiary method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researchers' obligation to cross-check quotations and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and research assistants have a duty to cross-check quotations with original materials to prevent misattribution entering the final manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodwin at times attributed failures to researchers' cross-checking; critics note final responsibility remains with the author, and systematic cross-checking is a best practice to ensure scholarly integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether prior reputable scholarship merits benefit of the doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's established record of 'valuable -- and blameless -- scholarly work' can be invoked to argue for leniency or benefit of the doubt in assessing alleged misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawrence Tribe and others argued Goodwin's prior work and lack of proven intent merited benefit of the doubt; other commentators reject differential treatment for established figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation of honors/prizes if won under false credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards and prizes may be reconsidered or asked to be revoked if evidence shows the work was obtained under false pretenses or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philip Nobile asked the Pulitzer Board to consider revoking Goodwin's 1995 prize on the grounds the prize was 'obtained under false credentials'; the Board historically declined similar requests (e.g., Alex Haley).
